title: The Christmas Stock Is Already Paid For. The Cash It Returns Won't Land Until January.
excerpt: Christmas stock gets ordered and paid for in November. The sales that repay it do not fully land until well into January, and sizing that gap now matters more than trading volume.
content:
By the middle of November, most retail, hospitality and wholesale businesses along the East Coast have already placed and paid for the stock that is meant to carry them through Christmas. The invoices landed weeks ago, often on thirty or sixty day terms that will run out before a single extra sale has been rung through the till.

The sales meant to repay that spend mostly land in a narrow four to six week window between late November and Christmas Eve, and a fair slice of what comes in during that window is already owed straight back out again, in casual wages for the extra trading days, in the next stock order, and in the BAS instalment and superannuation contributions that do not pause for the silly season.

This is not a cash flow problem caused by a slow month. It is a timing mismatch built into the trading calendar, and the businesses that get through it comfortably are usually the ones who sized the gap in dollar terms before November started, rather than assuming a strong trading month will cover it on its own.

The Gap Between Paying for Stock and Being Paid for It

Cash leaves the account the moment stock is ordered or delivered, well before it leaves the shelf. Cash only comes back once that stock sells, and even then there is a lag behind the sale itself: EFTPOS settlement timing, wholesale debtor terms, or a gift card that sits as a liability on the books until it is eventually redeemed. For a lot of owner-led businesses on the Queensland and New South Wales coast, that gap now stretches from a November order through to a January bank settlement, landing at exactly the same moment as obligations that do not wait for Christmas: the December BAS instalment, leave loading, and the first supplier invoice of the new trading year.

This isn't something a bookkeeper or BAS agent would normally flag, and that isn't a gap in their work. Their job is keeping the ledger accurate and the lodgements on time, which is exactly what keeps a business compliant. Sizing a seasonal cash timing gap before it lands is a commercial question sitting one layer above that, worth asking before the last order goes in rather than after the account runs tight in January.

The calculation worth doing before assuming trading volume will carry the business through is a genuine mapping of how much cash is sitting trapped between order and sale, across stock, debtor terms and supplier terms at the same time. That is close to the work a working capital unlock engagement is built to do for a business carrying this kind of seasonal pressure, and it produces a dollar figure rather than a feeling.

Why a Bigger December Doesn't Close the Gap

The instinct is understandable. December is the biggest trading month of the year for most of these businesses, so the thinking goes that cash will sort itself out once the sales start coming through. What that misses is that more stock bought to meet more demand means more cash leaving the account earlier, so volume alone widens the gap rather than closing it, unless the underlying terms, supplier payment windows, settlement speed, debtor terms, move with it. The pattern shows up hardest in tourism-driven retail and hospitality around the Gold Coast and similar coastal markets, where a strong December can multiply a normal month's cash timing gap several times over rather than smoothing it out.

Looking at this through a proper cash flow discipline lens, rather than through the P&L, is what separates businesses that trade through December comfortably from those that end January wondering where a profitable month's cash actually went.

What to Check Before the Last Order Goes In

Three things are worth confirming before placing the final Christmas stock order, and each one changes the size of the gap on its own.

  • The actual payment terms on that order, not the terms the business has always assumed it is on
  • Whether settlement timing from EFTPOS or online payment processing has shifted with any recent change in terminal or provider
  • Whether casual wages for the extra trading days are mapped against when the matching sales actually bank, not when they are rung through the till

None of this requires guesswork. It requires a dollar figure attached to the gap before the last order goes out, so the business knows whether it is managing a timing issue or quietly masking one. A conversation about that gap now costs far less than scrambling for a facility against a problem that has already landed in late January. If that is useful before the Christmas order goes in, book a discovery call while there is still time to act on it.

faqs.q: Why does paying for Christmas stock early cause a cash flow squeeze?
faqs.a: Stock is usually ordered and paid for weeks before the sales it funds actually happen, often on thirty or sixty day supplier terms. Those terms can run out before a single extra Christmas sale has come through the till, so the cash goes out well ahead of the cash coming back in, even in a strong trading month.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help manage Christmas trading cash flow?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO typically maps the actual dollar size of the gap between paying for stock and being paid by customers, across supplier terms, settlement timing and debtor terms at once, rather than leaving it to a general sense that trading volume will cover it. That figure then shapes how much cash can safely be spent elsewhere before Christmas trading starts.

faqs.q: Does a bigger December trading month guarantee more available cash?
faqs.a: Not on its own. More stock bought to meet more demand means more cash leaving the account earlier, so a stronger trading month often widens the timing gap rather than closing it, unless supplier terms or settlement speed change alongside the extra volume. Revenue and available cash can move in opposite directions during the same busy month.

faqs.q: When should an SME place its final Christmas stock order?
faqs.a: There is no single date that suits every business, but the order should go in only once the actual payment terms and the expected sales timing have been mapped against each other. A working capital unlock review is designed to produce exactly that figure before the order is locked in.

faqs.q: What is the cash conversion gap in a seasonal Australian business?
faqs.a: It is the time between cash leaving the account to pay for stock or services and cash returning once the matching sale is made and actually banked. Reviewing this properly through a cash flow discipline lens, rather than through the profit and loss statement, is what reveals the true size of the gap.

faqs.q: How can a Gold Coast or Sunshine Coast business manage Christmas cash flow?
faqs.a: Tourism-driven retail and hospitality on the Sunshine Coast often see the gap multiply several times over in December, since a bigger trading month means a bigger stock spend ahead of it. Sizing that gap in dollar terms before the last order goes in is the practical first step, well ahead of the busiest trading weeks of the year.
